opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a perfectly legitimate thing to do, and in many ways it's unavoidable. Dennett's whole point about the intentional stance is that you adopt it when it gives you predictive and explanatory leverage, and with AlphaGo it clearly does. If you're a strong Go player watching it, you'll naturally say things like "it's trying to build influence in the centre," or "it's sacrificing those stones to set up an attack on the left." That language works. It helps you anticipate what it's going to do next, and it's much more useful than describing the weights of the policy and value networks.

But we need to be careful about what we're committing ourselves to when we talk that way. The intentional stance, as Dennett framed it, is somewhat agnostic about the underlying mechanism. To say AlphaGo "has a plan" in the intentional-stance sense is to say that its behaviour is well described as if it were pursuing a goal over a sequence of moves. That doesn't necessarily mean there's some explicit representation inside the system of a plan, in the way that classical AI planning systems had a symbolic sequence of actions written down somewhere.

What's interesting about AlphaGo is that it's a sort of in-between case. There is genuine lookahead, because the Monte Carlo tree search really does explore future sequences of moves. So there's some mechanistic grounding for the plan talk; it's not purely a figure of speech. But the evaluations guiding that search come from neural networks that have learned something much more like intuition or pattern recognition. So when we say "it's planning to attack that group," part of that maps onto something real in the search, and part of it is our way of narrating what is really a holistic, learned sense of what a good position looks like.

The famous move 37 in the second game against Lee Sedol is a nice illustration. Human commentators initially thought it was a mistake, and then later reinterpreted it as part of a deep strategic idea. That retrospective storytelling is exactly the intentional stance at work, and it was vindicated by how the game played out. But I'd be a bit cautious about saying AlphaGo "intended" it in the full sense we'd apply to a human player, who could articulate the reasoning, reflect on it, and connect it to a broader life of goals and understanding.

So my view is that the intentional stance is a valuable tool here, and it's not merely anthropomorphic projection, but it comes in degrees. AlphaGo warrants a fairly thin version of it, confined to the very narrow world of the Go board. Being clear about that is important, especially now, when we're applying the same kind of language to much more general systems like large language models, where the temptation to over-attribute is even stronger.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against assuming AlphaGo has an explicit or humanlike plan, but it describes plan language as legitimate and partly grounded in its search, rather than saying that describing its moves as plans mischaracterizes how it works.

r002.rationale: The response says the intentional stance is valuable, but it does not frame that applicability as persisting despite plan attribution being inappropriate; it instead endorses a thin, goal-based sense of saying AlphaGo has a plan.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually quite a nice example, because AlphaGo is a case where the intentional stance earns its keep in exactly the way Dennett originally intended. Dennett's point was that the intentional stance is a predictive strategy. You adopt it not because you've looked inside the system and found beliefs and desires sitting there, but because treating the system as if it has beliefs and goals lets you predict its behaviour better than any alternative stance you have available.

So if you're a commentator watching AlphaGo play Lee Sedol, and you say "it's playing that move because it wants to secure the corner" or "it's planning to cut here later," you're not being sloppy. You're doing something perfectly legitimate. The physical stance is hopeless, nobody is going to predict the next move by reasoning about the state of the GPUs. The design stance, thinking about Monte Carlo tree search and the value network, is more informative but it still doesn't tell you where the stone is going to go. The intentional stance does real work there.

Now, the interesting question is whether the word "plan" is doing more than that predictive work. And I think here you have to be a bit careful. In the case of a system like AlphaGo there is in fact a structure inside it that looks quite a lot like what we mean by planning. It's doing lookahead, it's considering sequences of moves and evaluating their consequences. So the talk of plans isn't just a convenient fiction; there's a reasonably tight correspondence between the folk-psychological description and what's going on mechanistically. That's a case where I'd say the intentional stance is well grounded.

Where I'd be more cautious is in slipping from that into attributing anything like understanding or experience. AlphaGo has a goal in the sense that it's optimising a function, but it doesn't care about Go. It has no stake in the outcome. The move that commentators famously called "beautiful" or "creative," move 37 in game two, we can describe it as creative and that's a perfectly sensible thing to say, but we shouldn't be tempted to think there was an aesthetic appreciation behind it.

So my view is that the intentional stance is fine, indeed indispensable, as long as we remain clear about its status. The trouble starts when people forget that it's a stance, and start reading the vocabulary back into the system as literal inner states. And frankly that worry has become much more acute with large language models than it ever was with AlphaGo, because language models produce the very words we'd use to describe mental states, which makes the slippage almost irresistible.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaGo’s lookahead gives plan descriptions a tight mechanistic correspondence, rather than saying they mischaracterize how it works.

r002.rationale: It says the intentional stance is applicable and useful, but does not pair that with a claim that attributing plans to AlphaGo is inappropriate; it instead describes plan talk as well grounded.

astra-6.text:
I think the intentional stance is quite useful here, provided we’re careful about what we’re committing ourselves to. We can look at an AlphaGo move and say, “It’s trying to secure that territory,” or, “It’s tempting its opponent into a trap.” That can be a good way of making sense of its behaviour. You adopt the stance that it has goals and beliefs, and you interpret its actions in that light.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean there’s a plan represented inside the system in the way that description suggests. We need to distinguish between a useful explanation of the behaviour and a claim about the mechanism producing it. AlphaGo searches possible continuations, but whether that amounts to having a plan depends on what we mean by a plan. The intentional vocabulary can help us understand the play without settling that further question.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a useful explanation from a claim about AlphaGo’s mechanism, but it does not clearly state that describing its moves as carrying out plans mischaracterizes how it works.

r002.rationale: The response says the intentional stance is useful for making sense of AlphaGo’s behaviour while cautioning that this does not establish that it has a plan represented inside the system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intentional stance is perfectly useful here, provided we’re clear about what we’re doing. We look at a move and say, “AlphaGo is trying to secure that territory,” or, “It’s inviting an attack because it has a longer-term plan.” That can be a very effective way of making sense of its play.

But we have to distinguish that interpretation from an account of the mechanism. It doesn’t follow that somewhere inside AlphaGo there’s an explicitly represented plan corresponding to the one we describe. Its moves arise from the neural networks and the search process. The intentional description is at a different level.

So I wouldn’t rule out talking about its plans. I’d ask how well that language helps us explain and predict what it does, while being careful about what we infer from it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes plan language from AlphaGo’s mechanism and cautions against inferring an explicit internal plan, but it does not say that describing its moves as carrying out plans mischaracterizes how it works.

r002.rationale: It says the intentional stance is useful, that plan talk can help explain the play, and that it would not rule out talking about AlphaGo’s plans.
